scoreNote: Strong (5): grants that law cannot command belief while showing it solves countless problems by governing behavior and can even reshape attitudes over time, so the claim overstates its case; well organized.

sentences.text: We pass laws against almost everything we dislike, yet prejudice, greed, and cruelty persist, which gives the claim a surface plausibility.
It holds that many problems of modern society cannot be solved by laws and the legal system, on the reason that laws cannot change what lies in people's hearts and minds.

The reason captures a real limit of law, but it does not justify the sweeping claim, because laws solve a great many problems regardless of people's hearts, and can even change those hearts over time.
First, the reason rightly identifies something law cannot directly do.
A statute can forbid an act, but it cannot order a person to feel differently, and outlawing hatred does not by itself make anyone tolerant.
Laws against discrimination do not instantly erase prejudice, and a person forced to obey may go on resenting the rule in private.
Problems that live in attitudes — bigotry, selfishness, contempt — cannot be legislated out of existence by decree.
So the reason is correct that law has no direct power over the inner life.

sections.role: Body — But law solves problems by governing behavior

sentences.text: However, from the fact that law cannot command belief, it does not follow that it cannot solve society's problems.
A great many problems require not a change of heart but a change of behavior, and behavior is exactly what law can compel.
It does not matter whether a factory owner cares about clean air, only whether the law makes him stop polluting; the river grows clean either way.
Traffic laws, food-safety rules, and property rights solve enormous problems while caring nothing for what is in anyone's heart.
Much of modern life works smoothly precisely because law reliably governs conduct that good intentions alone could never coordinate.
The reason confuses changing minds with solving problems, when law solves countless problems by governing actions instead.
The point of a speed limit is not to make drivers virtuous but to keep them alive.
We do not need everyone to be virtuous, only to drive on the correct side of the road.

sections.role: Body — And law can change hearts over time

sentences.text: Moreover, the reason underestimates how law shapes the very hearts and minds it cannot directly command.
Behavior, once enforced, tends to reshape attitudes over time, as people come to accept and then to believe in what they were first merely required to do.
Laws ending segregation or extending rights were resented by many at first, yet within a generation they had helped transform public attitudes, not just public conduct.
Law teaches as well as commands, signaling what a society holds to be right and slowly bending opinion toward it.
Yesterday's grudging compliance has a way of becoming tomorrow's common sense.
Hearts follow habits more often than the reason allows.
In conclusion, the reason names a real limit but the claim overstates it.
Law cannot directly command belief, but it solves vast numbers of problems by governing behavior, and over time it can even change the hearts the reason says it cannot touch.
Laws are not the whole answer to society's problems, but they are far more of the answer than the claim admits.
